introduction-from-pdf-to-pipeline.core: Governance written in PDFs and wikis is ignored or applied inconsistently. Governance as code turns rules into automated checks and compliant-by-default modules, enforced in pipelines and at runtime.

first_principles.problem: A 40-page security standard sits on a shelf while teams launch public S3 buckets and untagged resources.
truths: People don't read long policy documents.

analogy.title: Safety rules in a binder vs. built into machines
analogy.story: Factory rules in a binder are ignored; guards built into machines protect everyone automatically.
analogy.breaks: Not every rule can be automated, so judgement-based policies still need humans.

example.title: A tagging policy
flow: PDF: 'All resources must be tagged with owner'
Code: CI fails Terraform plans missing owner tag

check.q: What's the main advantage of governance as code over policy documents?
check.a: Rules are enforced automatically and consistently in pipelines and at runtime, rather than depending on people reading and following documents.

the-vending-machine-model.core: Instead of letting teams hand-craft infrastructure, offer vending-machine modules: pre-approved, compliant Terraform modules or templates where you choose options (size, environment) and get a resource that already includes encryption, tagging, logging and network policy.

first_principles.problem: Every team writes its own S3 or RDS Terraform, each missing different security settings.
truths: Encoding standards once spreads them everywhere.
derivation: Build **modules** with secure defaults baked in.
**Version** them and publish in a registry.

analogy.title: A vending machine
analogy.story: You pick from approved options and get a sealed, safe product, instead of cooking it yourself.
analogy.breaks: Modules must evolve with needs, or teams fork them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every bucket is compliant without anyone thinking about it.

code.text:
module "bucket" {
  source  = "registry.acme.io/platform/s3-bucket/aws"
  version = "~> 3.2"
  name    = "orders-exports"
  env     = "prod"
  # encryption, versioning, block-public-access, tags, logging: built in
}

check.q: What's the 'vending machine' model in platform governance?
check.a: Offering pre-approved, compliant modules with limited safe options so teams get correct infrastructure by default.

drift-detection-combatting-clickops.core: ClickOps (manual console changes) causes drift: reality differs from code, compliance silently breaks and the next apply may revert or conflict. Detect drift with scheduled plans, AWS Config or GitOps reconcilers, and fix it through code.

first_principles.problem: Someone opens a security group to 0.0.0.0/0 in the console 'temporarily', and it stays that way for months.
truths: Code no longer describes reality after drift.
derivation: Run **scheduled `terraform plan`** in CI and alert on diffs.
Use **AWS Config / Azure Policy** rules for live resources.
Restrict **console write access**; provide break-glass with an audit trail.

analogy.title: A building inspector comparing the building to the plans
analogy.story: Unauthorised renovations are spotted and either documented or reversed.
analogy.breaks: Some drift is expected (autoscaling), so tune detection to ignore it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Manual changes are surfaced within a day.

code.text:
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=plan.out
if [ $? -eq 2 ]; then
  echo "Drift detected" && notify-slack "#infra-drift" plan.out
fi

check.q: What does `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` return when drift exists?
check.a: Exit code 2, meaning changes are pending (the infrastructure differs from the code).

preventive-governance-policy-checks-with.core: Preventive checks evaluate configurations before they're applied: OPA/Conftest on Terraform plans in CI, Kyverno or Gatekeeper at Kubernetes admission. They block violations (public buckets, missing encryption, privileged pods) with clear messages.

first_principles.problem: Modules help, but teams can still write raw resources that violate policy, and those are only discovered after deployment.
truths: Policies can be expressed as code.
Early feedback is fastest to fix.
derivation: Run **Conftest on the plan JSON** in CI.

analogy.title: A spell-checker that blocks sending
analogy.story: It catches errors before the message goes out, rather than after the recipient complains.
analogy.breaks: Too many blocking policies frustrate teams, so start with high-impact rules and use warnings first.

example.title: A Rego policy on a Terraform plan

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The violation is blocked at PR time with guidance.

code.text:
package terraform
deny[msg] {
  r := input.resource_changes[_]
  r.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  not r.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration
  msg := sprintf("%s must enable encryption (use module platform/s3-bucket)", [r.address])
}

check.q: Where can preventive policy checks run in a cloud-native pipeline?
check.a: In CI against Terraform plans (e.g. Conftest/OPA) and at Kubernetes admission (e.g. Kyverno or Gatekeeper).
